c-collier|2026-11-12|a8fb5aec|dd015cda6e.title: The Belmar Village SRA Document offers no accommodation for affordability to Very-low, Low, Moderate, or Gap income residents. Collier County’s approved Housing Demand Methodology assigns a maximum purchase price of $330,000 as the top level of affordably for households at the ceiling of the Gap income level. Households at the Moderate-Income level require products priced less than $275,000. Households at the Low-income level require products priced less than $150,000, and those at the Very-Low income require products priced less than that. The Economic Assessment indicates that 1,060 multifamily residential units in Bellmar Village may be priced near levels as to be affordable to some Moderate and Gap income households. The proposal does not seem to include any units that might be affordable for households at the Low or Very-Low income levels.

c-collier|2026-11-13|4e827bf5|1405efdd0d.title: 2026 Congestion Management Process | 5-2 5.2 CMP Strategy Evaluation Criteria The Congestion Management Committee plays a key role in identifying and recommending congestion management projects with the greatest potential benefit. The CMP Strategy Evaluation Criteria (see Appendix G) are used to evaluate project submittals for consistency with CMP Goals, Objectives, strategy toolbox, and hot spot congestion corridors. Projects developed consistent with the CMP Strategy Toolbox are submitted for funding consideration and evaluated by the CMC using the Strategy Evaluation Criteria. Based on this evaluation, the CMC provides recommendations to the MPO Board for project prioritization within the Transportation Improvement Program (TIP), consistent with the MPO’s most recent Long Range Transportation Plan (2050 LRTP). CMP projects that advance into project development and programming are typically funded with the Federal Surface Transportation Block Grant funds that are allocated to the Urbanized Area, consistent with the 2050 LRTP Cost Feasible Plan. c-collier|2026-11-13|4e827bf5|177528704e.title: 2026 Congestion Management Process | 1-1 1 Introduction The Congestion Management Process (CMP) is a data-driven, detailed, and systematic process conducted by the Collier Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO) to provide for the safe and effective management and operation of new and existing transportation facilities by using travel demand reduction and operational management strategies. The MPO is required by the federal government to implement a CMP as part of its routine planning efforts. Having a functional CMP that results in low-cost improvements or strategies benefits the regional transportation system by providing a defined approach for the MPO to address congestion concerns linked to transportation, livability, and land use. Projects identified through the CMP are coordinated with the MPO’s Long Range Transportation Plan (LRTP) in terms of identifying future revenue commitments and establishing planning consistency. 1.1 Federal Guidance The initial federal requirements for congestion management were introduced by the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act (ISTEA) of 1991 and were continued under its successor, the Transportation Equity Act for the 21st Century

For this event, the Calculator estimates an Economic Impact of $585,000. Staff utilizes the Board-approved Athletic Event & Tournament Application to evaluate whether the organization qualifies for funding. The canal receives stormwater from a large contributing basin and serves as the primary downstream receiving outfall for the Armand Beach, Johnson Beach, Hammock Beach, and Sea Colony communities. Stormwater in the Malacompra Canal is conveyed westward crossing SR A1A where it outfalls into the intracoastal water way (ICWW). The Canal is hydraulically connected to the ICWW and Atlantic Ocean, and upstream communities experience repeated flooding conditions during heavy precipitation events, tropical storms, dune breaching, and storm surge events. Additionally, Malacompra roadway is frequently being undermined and washed out during seasonal precipitation events and the banks of the canal are unstable and critically eroded. c-flagler|2026-11-16|fb7542d7|9127016c6d.title: As can be expected, the passage of Amendment 3 substantially changes our approach towards this Agreement. County staff contends that this Agreement far exceeds the equivalent share of the funding support provided to FHS by our municipal partners: we continue to fund the bulk of FHS operations through this Agreement. As proposed, Mandatory Services are limited to the required activities and should stay well-below the annual funding provided through this Agreement, while any excess funds (up to the $350,000 annual funding provided) can be used by FHS to provide the Additional Services that are part of the FHS mission and scope, but are not statutory or code requirements for the County to provide or fund. As the County prepares its FY 2027-28 budget, further service level cuts are likely, as well as another shift in the County's approach towards meeting its statutory and code obligations to provide core animal control services.

c-flagler|2026-11-16|fb7542d7|98030fe44a.title: Due to the limited time between the two meetings, County staff prepared a revised Agreement that constitutes a complete rewrite of the previous Agreement. In the proposed FY 2026-27 Agreement, funding is limited to $350,000 per year payable to the Flagler Humane Society (FHS) in equal monthly installments of $29,166.67, retroactive to October 1, 2026. Services provided by FHS to the County are divided into Mandatory Services (limited to those required by statute or by code, and including sheltering related to local emergencies) and Additional Services (primarily the sheltering of strays). A section was added by County staff that allows for FHS to request assistance from the Board for any extraordinary circumstances that occur, with the number of animals constituting an extraordinary circumstance changed from five or more animals to 25 or more animals.

Within Indian River County, the future land use map and zoning district designations establish a maximum density or intensity for all properties. Overall, density is an important factor in forming the character of a community and the preferred lifestyle of its residents. While higher densities may result in lower housing costs, higher across-the-board densities, do not always translate into lower housing prices. Consequently, the preferred method for reducing housing costs through increased density is to provide affordable housing density bonuses associated with affordable housing projects. Currently, Housing Policy 2.5 and LDR Section 911.14(4) provide affordable housing projects with up to a 20% density bonus over the maximum density established by the underlying land use designation. Currently, Housing Element Policy 2.5 and Section 911.14(4) of the LDRs provide for affordable housing density bonuses. Section 971.41(9) of the LDRs provides for small lot subdivisions for affordable housing. Approve Single Source Purchase of Remix Transit Planning Platform Item Summary: The agreement includes access to the Remix Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) platform, providing full planning and scheduling capabilities with continuous feature improvements, unlimited LeeTran user licenses, and dedicated premium Enterprise Support. Utilizing the single-source procurement method maintains continuity with existing County products and services, leveraging past investments in time and training while preventing service disruptions. By consolidating previously separate planning and scheduling software into a single, integrated platform, LeeTran reduces inefficient context switching and lowers overall subscription and maintenance costs by more than 10%. This three- year agreement locks in a modest 4% average annual increase, shielding the County from the 10%+ annual hikes standard across the transit software industry. This agreement will be 100% funded through FTA grant funds.

SUMMARY: As part of the FDACS routine agency review of Florida mosquito control programs participating in the “State Approved” mosquito control program, FDACS requests financial information from the mosquito control programs participating to determine what, if any, grant funding is allocated to each mosquito control program. As the total State grant is a finite amount, and is divided amongst the programs based on the tier they fall under, as determined by FDACS Form 13617, it is necessary that the County provide this financial report in order to maintain its participation in the “State Approved” mosquito control program. Since the Palm Beach County Mosquito Control Division’s budget exceeds $3M, it places the program in the State’s Tier I, which does not qualify for additional funding under Florida Administrative Code (F.A.C) 5E-13. There is no cost to the County. Countywide (FXM)

One of the funding methods available for capital improvements and essential services is to create the Municipal Service Benefit Unit (MSBU) and levy non-ad valorem special assessments on those properties that derive a direct benefit from the improvements. This type of assessment is based on benefit and collected along with property taxes using the uniform method pursuant to Section 197.3632 of the Florida Statutes. In order to preserve this funding option, it is necessary for the Board to adopt a resolution expressing its intent to use the uniform method of collecting commencing in November 2027. The resolutions must be considered at a duly advertised public hearing held prior to January 1, 2027. The MSBU process is typically started when a majority of property owners submit petitions to the County requesting that an MSBU be created. The mentioned resolutions do not in any way obligate the County to levy special assessments; rather, they simply satisfy the legal requirement, preserving the County's option to use a uniform method of collection if special assessments are levied. Plan Description, Membership and Plan Benefits, and Contribution Requirements Plan Description Full-time employees hired before January 1, 1996, are covered by the Florida Retirement System (FRS),a cost-sharing, multiple-employer defined benefit pension plan. The FRS was created by Chapter 121, Florida Statutes, to provide a defined benefit pension plan for participating public employees. The FRS was amended in 1998 to add the Deferred Retirement Option Program (DROP) under the defined benefit plan and amended in 2000 to provide a defined contribution plan alternative to the defined benefit plan for FRS members effective July 1, 2002. This integrated defined contribution pension plan is the FRS Investment Plan (INV). Chapter 112, Florida Statutes, established the Retiree Health Insurance Subsidy (HIS) Program, a cost-sharing multiple-employer defined benefit pension plan to assist retired members of any state-administered retirement system in paying the costs of health insurance. The FRS and HIS are administered by the Florida Department of Management Services, Division of Retirement. Deferred outflows of resources represent a consumption of net assets that applies to future periods and will not be recognized as an outflow of resources (expenditure or expense) until that applicable time. Deferred inflows of resources represent an acquisition of net assets that applies to future periods and will not be recognized as an inflow of resources (revenue) until that applicable time. The City reports three items that qualify as deferred outflows of resources on its government-wide and proprietary statements of net position - deferred outflows for pensions, deferred contribution for pensions and deferred outflows for OPEB. Defined Contribution Retirement Plan The City contributes to the General Employees' Defined Contribution Plan (DC Plan) for all full-time employees, other than certified police officers hired after January 1, 1996. All full-time and regular part-time general employees are eligible to participate upon employment. The DC Plan is administered by Mission Square Retirement Corporation. Benefit terms, including contribution requirements, for the DC Plan are established and may be amended by the City Commission. For each regular employee in the DC Plan, the City contributes 10% of annual salary. The City contributes 12% for Directors and 15% for the Commissioners and the City Manager. For the year ended September 30, 2025, the City recognized pension expense of $1,220,249. Employer contributions and earnings on those contributions are vested according to the following schedule: 20% after one year of service and 20% thereafter until fully vested. Nonvested City contributions are forfeited upon termination of employment. Such forfeitures are used to cover a portion of the DC Plan's administrative expenses. The most recent amendments to the City Charter were adopted by way of voters' referendum held on August 14, 2016. The legislative branch of the City is composed of a five (5) member elected Commission, including a City-wide elected Mayor. The City Commission is governed by the City Charter, and by state and local laws and regulations. The City Commission is responsible for the establishment and adoption of policy. The execution of such policy is the responsibility of the Commission-appointed City Manager. The accompanying financial statements present the City and its component unit, an entity for which the City is considered to be financially accountable. A blended component unit, although legally separate, is in substance, part of the City’s operations. The City has only one blended component unit, the Community Redevelopment Agency (the “CRA”). Resolution Number 2026-85: Write-Off of Uncollectible Accounts Policy City Attorney Taylor Tremel read the resolution by title only. Finance Director Lori Carr explained that the proposed policy formalizes the City’s existing practices for managing uncollectible receivables. The city had historically written off debts more than ten years old and proposed reducing that period to five years, consistent with industry practices. Because the write-off process had not been completed since 2018, the current review covered accounts dating from 2009 through September 30, 2021. The policy would authorize the City Manager to approve annual write-offs totaling up to $100,000 and the Finance Director to write off individual accounts of $25,000 or less. The policy applies to all City receivables, not just utility accounts, and included items such as business tax receipts and fire inspections. A write-off would be an accounting action and would not forgive the debt. This year, unencumbered funds being requested for roll-over are for very specific purposes. Staff are requesting approval for roll-over of the following unencumbered funds: General Fund - $67,179 • $13,206 – Professional Services • $53,973 – Contractual Services These funds are being requested to be carried over to fund the continuation of various consultants needed to continue to move the City forward with its Downtown Implementation Plan.

m-eustis|2026-11-19|be954cd5|801a48fbc9e.title: Background: Staff make every effort to encumber funds at the end of each fiscal year for projects that are expected to carry over into the following year. There are times, however, when adequate documentation is not available to encumber funds prior to the end of the fiscal year, but the funds do need to be carried over. In these instances, staff must request a budget amendment to carry these funds over. This Resolution provides the mechanism to amend the FY 2026/2027 budget to include any necessary remaining FY 2025/26 unencumbered funds for capital projects and consulting services. This year, unencumbered funds being requested for roll-over are for very specific purposes. Staff are requesting approval for roll-over of the following unencumbered funds: General Fund - $67,179 • $13,206 – Professional Services • $53,973 – Contractual Services These funds are being requested to be carried over to fund the continuation of various consultants needed to continue to move the City forward with its Downtown Implementation Plan.

The current method is a hand-counted audit of a randomly selected race and precincts chosen by the Canvassing Board and county judge. He said the second method utilizes technology called Clear Ballot, which takes a picture of each oval on every ballot and audits 100 percent of ballots. He said the equipment was separate from the machines used to tabulate votes. He said 32 of Florida’s 67 counties have adopted the technology, using county funding. Mr. Holland said the State wants all counties to use this technology and has provided funding for counties to purchase it by the end of the year. This bill would appropriate state funds to purchase the equipment. He said the amendment would identify the company as Clear Ballot, which is the only company certified to do post-election audits in the state.

m-mountdora|2026-11-18|1b8145a6|fefd5e75.title: Evans Park Renovation – Officially Awarded The City has received an official $1.5 million LWCF grant award for the Evans Park Renovation Project, which ranked 3rd statewide. Evans Park is one of Mount Dora's most popular waterfront destinations for residents and visitors. However, the park currently lacks basic amenities, including public restrooms and supporting infrastructure. These limitations impact everyday park use and require the City to rent equipment or secure sponsorships to provide temporary amenities during special events. The $3 million renovation project will address these longstanding needs through the addition of permanent restrooms, a new outdoor amphitheater, waterfront trail, picnic and gathering areas, and other park improvements. These improvements will enhance the everyday experience for residents while providing the infrastructure needed to better accommodate community events and reduce the City's reliance on temporary facilities.

At any regular municipal election held under the provisions of this charter, the candidates for the office of commissioner, in number equal to the number of commissioners to be elected, who shall have received the greatest number of votes cast, shall be declared elected. The candidate for Mayor receiving the greatest number of votes cast shall be declared elected. A tie between two ( 2) or more candidates for the office of commissioner shall be decided by a run-off election to be held within thirty ( 30) days of the certification of the results of the regular election. No runoff shall be held less than twenty-one ( 21) days after the regular election. The Firehouse Subs Public Safety Foundation will purchase and supply the equipment directly; therefore, the City will not be required to provide matching funds or incur an acquisition cost. Approval of the resolution will authorize acceptance of the award and allow the Department to place the equipment in service in accordance with applicable City procedures and award requirements. The project supports public safety and emergency-response readiness while avoiding a direct capital expense to the city.

m-palatka|2026-11-16|4e8ea773|bb6598022f.title: BACKGROUND St. Johns Avenue Streetscape Phase II is a downtown infrastructure project supported by City, CRA, and grant funding. The Transfer to Better Place Streetscape II account was included in prior fiscal years’ budget workshops and discussions as a planning allocation for anticipated streetscape improvements. The FY 2025–2026 Central Business District TIF budget included $911,684.00 in this account for transfer to the City’s Better Place Plan Fund. These allocations supported planning discussions but did not identify specific construction costs or establish the CRA’s funding commitment once the project moved into implementation. Staff has not located a CRA resolution or other formal Board action documenting the specific expenditure amounts committed by the CRA. Historically, shared projects such as Streetscape have lacked clear documentation of the City’s and CRA’s respective funding responsibilities and the separate approvals of each governing body. Presenting the proposed CRA expenditures to the CRA Board for approval clarifies the Board’s role in approving CRA funding and creates a public record of the CRA’s contribution.

However, even with this substantial income, the Pier still relies on city subsidies for the remainder of its funding. The City of St. Petersburg (City) was allocated $159,884,000 per the Allocation Announcement Notice (90 FR 4759) published on January 16, 2025. On June 12, 2025, City Council approved the CDBG-DR Action Plan for the use of the federal grant funds (Resolution No. 2025-327) which allocated $6,000,000 to the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program. HUD approved the City’s Action Plan in August 2025 and executed the City’s Grant Agreement in February 2026. Through extensive public input and Unmet Needs and Mitigation Needs Assessments in the Action Plan, the City determined the need to create the Non-Profit Community Support Services (NPCSS) program to address the increased need for essential community services as a result of the qualifying disasters. m-tallahassee|2026-11-18|6c640e76|c7f4ce.title: Section 420.9075 Florida Statute and Chapter 67 -37, Florida Administrative Code, states: “A county or an eligible municipality may not exceed the 5 percent limitation on administrative costs, unless its governing body finds, by resolution, that 5 percent of the local housing distribution plus 5 percent of program income is insufficient to adequately pay the necessary costs of administering the local housing assistance plan.” Section 420.9075 Florida Statute and Chapter 67-37, Florida Administrative Code, further states: “The cost of administering the program may not exceed 10 percent of the local housing distribution plus 5 percent of program income deposited into the trust fund, except that small counties, as defined in s. 120.52(19), and eligible municipalities receiving a local housing distribution of up to $350,000 may use up to 10 percent of program income for administrative costs. ” The applicable local jurisdiction has adopted the above findings in the resolution attached as Exhibit E.

m-tavares|2026-11-18|953110a1|0a0b4f2fca.title: SUMMARY: The City of Tavares is requesting $75,000 to amend its ongoing Clean Water Facility Plan (CWFP) by evaluating reclaimed water reuse augmentation alternatives. This work will support Water Reclamation Facility (WRF) upgrades needed to meet Florida’s advanced wastewater treatment requirements and accommodate future growth. Although the City routinely beneficially reuses treated effluent under its discharge permit, the current CWFP evaluates only treatment processes and does not address long- term reuse needs. The amendment will forecast seasonal reuse demand over 20 years, compare it with projected wastewater flows, and identify supply-demand gaps. The City will evaluate up to three augmentation alternatives and prepare planning-level cost estimates to establish reliable, sustainable reuse capacity. The resulting amended SRF Facility Plan will be submitted to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection for approval, positioning the City to pursue future funding and implement a cost-effective capital project. Potential solutions include upgrading the existing WRF to increase reuse supply or constructing pipelines to convey water from a nearby surface water source.

The City issued Invitation to Bid (ITB) No. 2026-10 for the Tidal Valve Program on July 9, 2026, with bids opened on August 20, 2026. The project generally includes installation of inline backflow check valves at stormwater outfalls throughout the City, together with associated drainage structure modifications, pipe cleaning and repairs, pollution-retardant baffles, roadway and landscape restoration, and other related work. Following review of the bids, Southern Underground Industries, Inc. was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder. The final Schedule of Values establishes a construction amount of $1,354,231.30.
